item.title: Live: Rescuers struggle to reopen Gyirong Port route
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
President Xi Jinping urges all-out rescue, relief efforts after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Level-II emergency response activated after mudslide hits border port in Xizang 16 dead, 546 missing after mudslide hits border port in Xizang On Saturday, two helicopters from the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command were urgently deployed to the hardest-hit area near the Gyirong Port, carrying food, medicine and rescue equipment to frontline rescuers. China is delivering a package of assistance to Nepal, including emergency cash assistance and humanitarian aid, following a severe cross-border disaster triggered by a glacial collapse, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Saturday. During a phone conversation with Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, Wang said disaster relief supplies provided by China would soon arrive in Kathmandu. Chinese tunnel rescue experts have been divided into two teams and dispatched respectively to the disaster-hit area and Kathmandu to assist with rescue operations. China has also shared with Nepal important information, including imagery, satellite and hydrological data from the disaster-hit area, as well as early-warning information on barrier lakes upstream, Wang said. Regarding Nepali citizens stranded on the Chinese side, he said China has made proper arrangements for them and will help them return to Nepal as soon as possible. Wang said the sudden glacial collapse in the China-Nepal border area had triggered severe mudslides, causing significant casualties and leaving people missing on both sides. He described it as the most serious cross-border disaster between the two countries in recent years, saying the complexity and difficulty of rescue and relief operations were unprecedented. While carrying out emergency rescue operations on its own side, China immediately extended a helping hand to support Nepal's disaster relief efforts, Wang said. Wang thanked Nepal for its efforts to rescue and evacuate Chinese citizens in Nepal and expressed hope that the Nepali side would continue such efforts. In the face of the disaster, he called on China and Nepal to stand firmly together, work hand in hand to overcome the difficulties and demonstrate through concrete actions their traditional friendship across the Himalayas. Khanal expressed sincere gratitude for China's emergency humanitarian assistance. He said that although both Nepal and China had been affected by the disaster, China had overcome its own difficulties to immediately convey sympathies and provide assistance to Nepal, fully demonstrating the high level of Nepal-China relations. Nepal will continue to work closely with China and make every effort to rescue Chinese nationals who remain trapped or missing, while working together to rescue missing foreign nationals, Khanal said. He added that Nepal is ready to strengthen cooperation with China in post-disaster reconstruction, disaster prevention and mitigation, and climate change response, and to further advance the strategic partnership of cooperation between the two countries. On August 29, land search teams from Lhasa fire and rescue mobile detachment conducted search‑and‑rescue operations under arduous conditions in the core disaster zone of Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. Traversing slick ground blanketed by deep suction‑heavy mud, rescuers, tethered by ropes, forge ahead in coordinated moves. Thousands of netizens have left messages of solidarity on the social media platform of the border inspection station in Xizang autonomous region that was hit by a devastating mudslide on Wednesday. Communications with members of staff at the Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang have been lost since it was hit by a mudslide originating in Nepal on Wednesday. On Saturday, the official WeChat account of the Xizang general station of entry-exit border inspection, which the Gyirong Port is subordinate to, shared an update revealing it had been flooded with messages, prayers and good wishes from netizens across China since Wednesday, many reading simply "We're waiting for you to come back." The post also featured a short video clip showing officers at the Gyirong Port. As of Saturday afternoon, it had received more than 284,000 thumbs-up and been forwarded over 4,600 times, with about 6,000 comments. A netizen using the nickname "Nanshanxianke" commented on the video, "They (the station officers) guard the nation's gateway with their lives," drawing responses from others writing, "May a miracle be with them, and may they all return safely." "They are the pillars of their families. This is a tragedy for so many households," wrote a netizen named "Hezhouhuaer". Another user, who goes by the name "Wuxibancaijiejie", posted a photo of a young woman in uniform sitting on a sofa, with a caption that read: "We are all waiting for you to come back. You have never made us worry during your more than a decade of service at the border. We believe you will return safely this time too. Your 1-year-old son calls 'mom' every day." Netizen "Yanjun" wrote, "Tears welled up in my eyes. Though we are strangers to one another, our hearts are connected. You are the people I respect the most." A posted reply from the Xizang station read: "We seek no grand ode to heroism — only a miracle that endures. May it come, and may our fellow officers return safely." MACAO -- The Macao Special Administrative Region government has decided to donate 30 million yuan ($4.42 million) through the Macao Foundation to Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region to support rescue and post-disaster recovery, the Macao SAR Government Information Bureau said Saturday. Macao SAR Chief Executive Sam Hou-fai recently conveyed condolences to the autonomous region, mourning those who lost their lives and expressing sympathy to their families and people affected by the disaster. The Macao SAR government said it will make every effort to provide medical and other assistance needed in the affected areas and support post-disaster recovery. It called on all sectors of Macao society to extend assistance to Gyirong in Xizang and help affected residents resume normal life as soon as possible. Chinese tunnel experts have arrived in Nepal's mudslide-hit region to assist rescue efforts at a damaged hydropower tunnel following a request from the Nepali government, the Ministry of Emergency Management announced on Saturday. Departing by helicopter from Gyirong county in Xizang autonomous region, which lies just across the Nepali border, the first group of five Chinese tunnel specialists arrived at the disaster site in Nepal late Saturday afternoon and immediately began rescue operations at the tunnel. Gyirong county also suffered heavy losses as a result of the mudslide. To reinforce the team and meet operational needs, Chinese authorities are rushing an additional four experienced tunnel experts to Nepal, a ministry statement said. Emergency response and power supply restoration efforts are continuing after the severe mudslide at Gyirong border port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, according to the Shigatse branch of the State Grid Xizang Electric Power Company. As of 9 am on Saturday, one tower base station had begun supplying power to the newly constructed emergency warehouse, two key parking lots, and 32 resettlement tents at the relocation site in Gyirong township. Maintenance personnel were dispatched for inspections of equipment, substations and power supply lines, according to the company, dealing with three hazards through live-line work. A total of 29 ground inspection teams were deployed, using a combination of drone aerial inspections and manual ground verification to conduct four special inspections and one infrared temperature measurement on 48 road crossings and densely populated areas. Maintenance of the port power station channels and black-start drills were also completed. A total of 126 repair personnel, 13 generator trucks, 52 generators and 48 lighting equipment units had arrived in the township by Saturday, with another 16 lighting devices supplied by the company on standby in Gyirong county. HONG KONG -- John Lee Ka-chiu, chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, said on Saturday that HK$50 million ($6.37 million) has been earmarked from the Disaster Relief Fund following a mudslide that hit the Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region. In a post on social media, Lee expressed deep sadness over the disaster, mourning the victims and extending his sincere sympathies to those affected and the bereaved families. Lee hoped that the rescue operations would proceed safely and smoothly, and that the affected residents would receive timely support to overcome the hardships. He added that the Disaster Relief Fund Advisory Committee will process funding applications expeditiously. "Is anyone there?" In Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, rescue workers are calling out for signs of life, their voices echoing around the mudslide-devastated valleys. Days after a mudslide tore through Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, search and rescue teams are racing against difficult and hazardous terrain to comb through core areas, maintaining continuous and uninterrupted operations. After a mudslide struck Gyirong border port, Shigatse, Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region, engineering crews made robust efforts to reinforce power facilities, ensuring uninterrupted telecommunication connections for rescue operations. Comprehensive efforts are in motion to reestablish road connectivity to Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, following a devastating mudslide originating in Nepal. The calamity has inflicted severe damage on the G216 highway, the main access route to the port, creating significant obstacles for rescue and relief operations. Zhu Feng, chief engineer at China Anneng Construction Group's Chengdu rescue base, said on Saturday that they deployed 60 technicians and 28 pieces of heavy equipment, including excavators and loaders, to the affected area on the G216 highway leading to the port. Following a disaster risk assessment and monitoring of surrounding hazards, members from the group, a State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, commenced operations to clear a 2-kilometer damaged section near the port, with the goal of facilitating the efficient implementation of subsequent rescue and disposal efforts, Zhu added. On Aug 29, a massive mudslide cut off Highway G216 near Gyirong Port, Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. To secure this vital rescue passage, the State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng Construction Group has deployed 60 specialists and 28 sets of machinery to reopen the roughly 2-kilometer road, with the company’s teams assessing and monitoring potential risks and hazards. Efforts to reinforce power and base station infrastructure are advancing to ensure uninterrupted communication for rescue operations following a severe mudslide at a border port in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. On Saturday morning, engineering crews shored up power facilities, guaranteeing uninterrupted telecommunications connections for relief operations. "Our goal is to ensure that communications keep pace with road clearance, rolling out power facilities and network coverage simultaneously, so that the telecommunications network truly becomes a lifeline for rescue and relief operations," said Kelsang Norbu, manager of the operations and maintenance department for China Tower's Xizang branch, one of the world's largest telecommunications tower infrastructure service providers. He told China Daily that the immediate priority on Saturday was strengthening auxiliary infrastructure, particularly boosting power supply to facilitate broader network coverage. The team working on reinforcing communication links include members from China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom. Days after a mudslide tore through Gyirong Port, Xizang autonomous region, search and rescue teams are racing against difficult and hazardous terrain to comb through core areas, maintaining continuous and uninterrupted operations. On Saturday morning, the rescue teams dispatched by the Ministry of Emergency Management and the National Fire and Rescue Administration, continued to search through debris at the mudslide-hit site near Gyirong Port. LHASA -- Seven people had been killed, and 554 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued as of 1 am on Saturday after a mudslide struck the Gyirong Port along the China-Nepal border in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region, according to the region's emergency management department. A total of 2,141 rescue workers and 86 specialists from natural resources and other relevant fields have been deployed to the disaster area. With specialized equipment, they have stepped up inspections for geological hazards across surrounding slopes, roads and other critical zones. A five-person monitoring post has been set up to keep the barrier lake under constant observation and guard against potential secondary disasters. In addition, 1.02 kilometers of road have been cleared and reopened to traffic. The mudslide, which occurred on the Nepalese side, struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong county of Xizang on Wednesday morning. Rescue and road-clearing operations are advancing into the heart of mudslide-stricken Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, where vehicles lie twisted and mangled by the force of the disaster. Since Saturday morning, teams from the Ministry of Emergency Management and National Fire and Rescue Administration have been actively working in the disaster-stricken areas near the Gyirong border port. As excavators assist in the effort, team members are conducting thorough inspections, carefully navigating the region's challenging terrain. Workers from China Anneng Construction Group, a State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, told China Daily that they are approximately 1.8 to 2 kilometers from the port, an area severely affected by the massive mudslide that struck Nepal on Wednesday, resulting in significant casualties. Rescue teams are continuing to push toward the core mudslide-hit area in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, through forested mountains and murky waters, as damaged roads, disrupted utilities, frequent rainfall and an overflowing barrier lake continue to complicate the dogged search for missing people. Around 4:30 pm on Friday, six members from the first response team of the Xizang fire and rescue brigade and 15 members — along with one search-and-rescue dog — from the first response team of the Sichuan fire and rescue brigade reached the Gyirong border port, which bore the maximum brunt of the deadly mudslide on the Chinese side. These were the first professional rescue teams to reach the core area, Xinhua News Agency reported. Even as damaged roads, disabled communication systems and snapped power supplies hindered rescue and relief efforts a day after the disaster, workers remained determined to achieve results. They cleared and repaired overnight a nearly 1-kilometer stretch of a 2.8-km approach road to the border gate. Jigme Dorje, Party chief of the Nyalam maintenance section of the Shigatse highway development center, said eight machines — including four excavators and four loaders — and more than 20 workers were clearing and repairing the road. Local volunteers and enterprises are also supporting their efforts, he added. Xia Mingyong, from the Lhasa fire and rescue mobile detachment, said the team's rescuers were advancing by land and water. "On land, we are mainly moving toward the border port on foot. In water, we are using rubber boats to reach the severely affected port area," he said. On Friday, a barrier lake that formed upstream of Gyirong port topped 90 million cubic feet of water, up from the estimated 50-70 million cubic feet recorded on Thursday, raising the risk of secondary disasters, agencies reported. The overflow sparked panic and warnings from Nepalese authorities, leading to rescue operations being suspended in Nepal for about three hours. The risk of the lake bursting also prompted rescue personnel and vehicles on the Chinese side to be on standby in a safe area, China Central Television reported. Both sides resumed rescue operations after the threat eased. "By noon, as the risk posed by the upstream barrier lake was deemed manageable, rescue operations for the Gyirong mudslide disaster quickly resumed and were stepped up," CCTV said. According to a news release by Chinese authorities, a total of 2,096 rescuers, including firefighters, police personnel and medical workers, have been deployed in the county. More than 300 vehicles, drones and two satellite communications vehicles are being used for rescue, evacuation guidance, reconnaissance and frontline communications. Furthermore, 32 experts are conducting on-site surveys of barrier lakes to support decision-making, while a five-member observation post has been set up to monitor the two lakes in real time and prevent secondary disasters. Fire and rescue teams have set up three task groups to reach the hardest-hit area by rubber boats and by scaling mountains on foot, and for using drones for reconnaissance and supply deliveries. Small teams mobilized in advance are also monitoring the core disaster area and the barrier lake with drones and binoculars. Local authorities said 499 affected residents have already been resettled and 555 stranded tourists evacuated. Shigatse has allocated more than 15,000 relief items, with additional rescue supplies to be allocated based on actual need. Wednesday's disaster was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal. The ice-and-rock collapse evolved into a massive debris flow and then into a forceful mudslide, destroying everything in its path, including the border port. Meteorological authorities have forecast frequent rainfall through Sunday and warned of possible secondary disasters. Contact the writers at yangzekun@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Stronger rescue efforts in Xizang urged
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
Stronger rescue efforts in Xizang urged Xi sends message of condolence to Nepal over mudslide Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, chaired a Party leadership meeting on Friday to deliberate and make arrangements to strengthen rescue and relief efforts in the Xizang autonomous region, where the Gyirong land port along the China-Nepal border and its surrounding areas were hit by a catastrophic mudslide on Wednesday morning. At the start of the meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, Xi, who is also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, and other leaders observed a moment of silence to mourn the victims of the disaster. As of press time on Friday, five people were confirmed dead and more than 500 still missing in Gyirong county in Xizang's Shigatse. Nepal has reported 579 deaths, while more than 1,900 people are missing there. On Friday, Xi sent a message of condolence to Nepal's President Ram Chandra Poudel over the mudslide, which was triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse. On behalf of the Chinese government and people, Xi expressed deep condolences for the deceased and offered sincere sympathies to the bereaved families, the injured and the people in the disaster-stricken areas. During the Political Bureau meeting, it was noted that emergency rescue operations in Gyirong county in Xizang's Shigatse have so far been carried out in a swift, orderly and well-coordinated manner under the strong leadership of the CPC Central Committee, with comprehensive efforts underway for the resettlement of affected people and for proper handling of the aftermath. The disaster occurred in a severely cold plateau region with steep valleys, variable weather and many surrounding glaciers and glacial lakes, and potential geological hazards are posing significant challenges to emergency rescue operations, the meeting said. It was emphasized that all relevant authorities and departments should take resolute and effective measures for rescue-related work, search and rescue plans should be formulated in a scientific manner, and every effort should be made to search for and rescue all missing Chinese and foreign nationals. The Party leadership also underlined the need to strengthen multi-department joint consultations, enhance monitoring and early-warning systems, and closely track the stability of the barrier lake and surrounding mountains to effectively prevent secondary disasters. It is essential to reinforce the management of on-site personnel to ensure safety throughout the rescue process, the meeting said, urging proper arrangements for the affected people and meticulous attention to post-disaster relief and support. China will provide emergency aid to the disaster-hit areas in neighboring Nepal and carry out international rescue cooperation, the Party leadership decided. The importance of balancing development and security, preparing for the extreme and worst-case scenarios, and bearing a strong sense of political responsibility and constant vigilance to ensure security and stability in all aspects of work was emphasized at the meeting. Meanwhile, Xi, in his condolence message to Poudel, noted that China and Nepal are connected by mountains and rivers and share a common destiny. China is willing to actively aid Nepal in its rescue efforts and provide support and assistance to the best of its capability, he said. Xi expressed his belief that the people of both countries will be able to work together to prevail over the disaster and rebuild their homes as soon as possible. Premier Li Qiang also sent a message of condolence to Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah. Entrusted by Xi, the Chinese premier traveled to Gyirong county on Thursday to guide rescue and emergency response efforts. While assessing the ground situation and meeting with rescue teams, Li emphasized the need to put the people and their lives above all else and spare no effort in carrying out rescue operations and emergency response work. He said that as long as there is a glimmer of hope, every effort should be made to search for and rescue still those missing. Li later visited temporary shelters for affected residents and conveyed President Xi's concern and care to them. The premier emphasized the need to continue dispatching and transporting disaster-relief supplies and ensure the basic living needs of evacuated and relocated residents. Li heard reports from local authorities and relevant departments about the disaster, and discussed further efforts in rescue and emergency response measures. He highlighted the need to coordinate the deployment of rescue forces and equipment, strengthen on-site unified command and thoroughly ascertain the status of missing persons to conduct effective rescues. Transparency in the release of information regarding the disaster and rescue operations is crucial, he added. caodesheng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Services trade to benefit from policy tailwinds
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
Services trade to benefit from policy tailwinds China's trade in services, underpinned by robust growth in knowledge-intensive service-sector exports and burgeoning inbound tourism, is set to benefit from further policy and market developments in the second half, officials and experts said, pointing to the sector's emergence as a key engine of foreign trade growth. Their remarks came ahead of the five-day 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services, which is scheduled to open in Beijing on Sept 9, as the country doubles down on efforts to broaden access to its vast services market amid rising protectionist barriers and heightened economic uncertainty. "This year's fair will bring together some 90 countries and international organizations, with more than 1,800 companies set to exhibit on-site," said Yan Dong, vice-minister of commerce, at a news conference on Friday. More than 90 companies and institutions will unveil new technologies, products and services spanning information and communications technology, fintech and digital healthcare, some of which will be making their global debuts or their first showings in China, Yan said. In order to strengthen the competitive edge of Chinese services in global markets, this year's fair will, for the first time, feature a promotion and roadshow area dedicated to overseas expansion services, said Tang Wenhong, vice-mayor of Beijing. China's two-way trade in services posted solid growth in the first half, with total imports and exports rising 8.3 percent year-on-year to 3.8 trillion yuan ($560.4 billion), the Ministry of Commerce said. Services exports surged 17.6 percent, providing a strong boost to foreign trade growth. Notably, knowledge-intensive services exports rose 12.8 percent to 805.67 billion yuan, accounting for 53.5 percent of the total. "With knowledge-intensive services now accounting for more than half of the total, China's services exports have reached an inflection point and are moving further up the value chain," said Bai Wenxi, vice-chairman of the China Enterprise Capital Union, adding that digital technology and artificial intelligence are accelerating the shift, with digital services emerging as a new growth engine. The sector is also set to receive further policy support in the July-December period, as national demonstration zones for the innovative development of trade in services and other measures begin to deliver results, said Yan, adding, "China's trade in services is expected to remain on a positive trajectory this year, with services exports continuing to grow strongly." Wang Peng, a researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said China's expanding services sector is also creating new opportunities for foreign companies, given the country's vast market and well-developed industrial ecosystem. "Foreign companies can leverage their expertise to play a greater role in China's expanding services market and benefit as consumer spending shifts toward higher-quality services," Wang said. Falkor AS, a Norway-based industrial intelligence provider serving the global energy sector, will make its fifth appearance at CIFTIS this year, showcasing its solutions, real-world applications and the results of its work with industry partners, said Wu Haifeng, Falkor's senior vice-president. Norway will be the guest country of honor at this year's fair. Norwegian businesses hope to use the occasion to build new partnerships in China, said Wu, who is also vice-chairman of the Norwegian Business Association China. "Over the next five years, we will continue to increase our investment in China, deepen local partnerships and use industrial intelligence to boost operational performance and advance the green transition of the energy sector," Wu said. Beijing, this year's host of CIFTIS, is also opening its services sector wider. A citywide data-export negative list now covers nine sectors, including medical devices, and opening-up pilots are underway in value-added telecommunications and biotechnology areas, said Tang, the city's vice-mayor. zhangchenxu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China unveils plan to expedite major projects
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
China unveils plan to expedite major projects Policymakers intensify efforts to expand effective investment, stimulate demand China is accelerating the construction of major State-backed projects and building a pipeline for 2027, as policymakers intensify efforts to expand effective investment, stimulate domestic demand and channel spending toward strategic infrastructure and technology. The National Development and Reform Commission, the country's top economic regulator, said on Friday it is urging local authorities to coordinate physical construction with supportive institutional reforms under the "two priorities" initiative, which focuses on implementing major national strategies and building the nation's security capacity in key areas, while ensuring the prudent and efficient use of funds. The aim is to expedite project delivery and generate tangible "physical workload" on the ground as quickly as possible, Li Chao, deputy director of the NDRC's policy research office, told a news conference in Beijing. The NDRC is stepping up planning for a 2027 project pipeline, Li added. The push comes as China actively transitions toward higher-quality growth, channeling capital into advanced manufacturing, new infrastructure and green transitions while reducing reliance on traditional real estate-driven expansion. The NDRC said it is coordinating with relevant departments to accelerate the deployment of new policy-based financial instruments and expand support for private investment and optimize financing mechanisms for the "six networks" initiative. The network program covers water, power, computing, next-generation communications, urban pipelines and logistics. Separately, S&P Global Ratings affirmed China's sovereign credit ratings at "A+/A-1" with a stable outlook on Friday. The agency said proactive fiscal support should help keep growth above 4 percent over the next one to two years, as the economy steadily navigates ongoing property adjustments. Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities, said the heightened policy focus on the "six networks" indicates that key strategic projects are swiftly moving from the drawing board to the construction phase. "As preparatory work concludes and construction picks up pace, infrastructure investment is poised to accelerate markedly in the second half of the year, providing solid support for overall fixed-asset investment," Luo said. Xiong Yuan, chief economist at Guosheng Securities, said the "two priorities" initiative and network infrastructure will systematically address the shortage of high-return, bankable projects at the local level, though he noted that the structural transition toward emerging industries will be a steady, compounding process. Su Jian, director of Peking University's National Center for Economic Research, said the projects under the "two priorities" initiative carry strategic, nationwide significance. By combining physical construction with institutional and market reforms, such initiatives provide immediate support to macroeconomic stability while laying a durable foundation for technological innovation, future industries and new quality productive forces. The tangible benefits of targeted investment are already visible in strategic sectors such as semiconductors. NDRC data showed that investment in integrated circuit manufacturing in the first seven months of the year rose 11.5 percent year-on-year. Among listed companies in the sector that had disclosed interim results by Thursday, aggregate revenue rose 12.8 percent year-on-year and net profit increased 99 percent, while research and development spending increased 13.4 percent, according to the NDRC. Roger Sheng, vice-president at US research firm Gartner, said China is seeking a more flexible policy framework to mobilize resources in the integrated circuit sector while avoiding wasteful investment. Chinese companies are narrowing the technological gap with global leaders, Sheng said, though bottlenecks remained in areas including lithography equipment. Contact the writers at lijing2009@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Lotus festivals reveal imperial charm
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
For many Beijingers, the lotus is not just a flower in a park; it is a part of summer. Families plant lotus tubs in the courtyards of old homes, while the flower's leaves and seeds are used to enhance the nourishing quotient of homemade porridge. This year, however, the city's lotus season is bigger than the courtyards. Thirteen parks, including Beihai Park, the Summer Palace and Yuanmingyuan Ruins Park, are hosting lotus festivals, which lean into the flower's imperial history. Visitors can watch performances in ancient style, take part in ceremonies built around lotus-scented teas, join stamp-collection activities and try royal-themed drinks. The bloom is drawing foreign photographers and vloggers in droves. Canadian photographer Madelyn Arnold shared her photos on the Beijing municipal government's website, in the "Beijing Through Foreigners' Lens" section. "I was fully immersed in the beauty of the blooming lotus flowers and the good fortune they represent," Arnold wrote. Scottish photographer Bruce Connolly, who has lived in China for 39 years, posted an image of lotuses blooming against the backdrop of white clouds over Shichahai on his WeChat Moments and LinkedIn account. Shichahai is a well-preserved traditional residential area in Beijing's Xicheng district, and one of the busiest tourist spots in the city. "Walking along the waterway on the Central Axis toward Yinding Bridge, then along Qianhai, the lotus lane is unforgettable, especially when photographing at sunset," Connolly said. At Beihai Park, one of China's earliest and best-preserved imperial gardens, lotus flowers have bloomed for more than 800 years. Zhang Meng, a seasoned docent there, said that locals treat lotus viewing as a shared ritual. "For typical Beijingers, visiting Beihai to appreciate lotus flowers in the cool summer or breezy early autumn is a shared passion," she said. In the early 2000s, the park introduced more than 3,000 lotus plants, some grown from seeds that had been sent to space as part of a national scientific project. Today, lotus-themed souvenirs and lotus-flavored drinks at the park's cafes have become hugely popular. Serbian vlogger Katarina Stojanovic, a graduate from Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, pays attention to how the plant is used. She noted that Empress Dowager Cixi of the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) enjoyed summer drinks made with lotus seeds, which are known for their medicinal value. Stojanovic tried a lotus-flavored drink at the Summer Palace. "It was so refreshing and cooling," she said. "The lotus is not just for appreciation; it serves both medicinal and culinary purposes. Lotus seeds nourish the heart, calm the mind and strengthen the spleen." For Connolly, the Scottish photographer, the appeal is simple. "Although it's been 39 years since I first set out to discover and photograph Beijing, the passion still remains within me," he said. "Walking in the city, there is always something fascinating to capture through the lens."

item.title: Local for local: a paradigm shift for business
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
Local for local: a paradigm shift for business German companies compete, innovate, and develop in China to sharpen their global competitiveness. Germany's economy has returned to growth in 2026, but whether Europe's largest economy has finally left years of stagnation behind remains far from certain. According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's real GDP expanded by 0.4 percent quarter-on-quarter in the first three months of the year and by another 0.2 percent in the second quarter. While the figures point to a tentative recovery after years of economic weakness, a combination of domestic constraints and external shocks continues to cast a shadow over the outlook for the second half of the year. The situation is being worsened by climate change, with heat and drought sending water levels plunging on the Rhine, which is one of Europe's most important commercial waterways. Near Cologne, the receding water levels that have disrupted inland shipping have been so severe they exposed a 500-kilogram unexploded United States World War II bomb. Germany's energy-intensive industries are facing another squeeze as conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and raw material costs. The Leibniz Institute for Economic Research at the University of Munich (ifo Institute) has estimated that the energy shock alone could shave about 0.4 percentage points off German economic growth this year, while exports to the US fell 14.2 percent month-on-month in June with uncertainty created by US tariff and trade policies. Eberhard J. Trempel, director-general of the German Global Trade Forum Berlin, has argued that Germany's competitiveness is being weighed down by high energy and raw material costs, heavy tax and social-security burdens, high labor costs, slow approval procedures, and a shortage of skilled workers. Against this backdrop, German businesses are searching more urgently for new sources of growth. Strategy by increments There has been no single declaration that German industry has found a new answer to its problems at home. Instead, the direction becomes visible through a series of major corporate decisions made in different sectors for different reasons. On March 26, German chemical giant BASF officially inaugurated its newly built Verbund site in Zhanjiang city, Guangdong province, a sprawling industrial complex covering around 4 square kilometers and representing an investment of 8.7 billion euros ($10.15 billion). The investment is particularly striking because it comes as Germany's chemical industry has struggled with high energy costs, subdued demand, and concerns about industrial competitiveness at home. "Zhanjiang shows what the future of chemistry looks like: efficient, digital, and sustainable by design," BASF CEO Markus Kamieth said at the inauguration. The project was completed on schedule and below its original budget, and the site is powered entirely by renewable electricity, and most of what it produces will be sold directly to customers in China under BASF's "local-for-local" strategy. "This investment shows confidence in the world's largest chemical market in the long run," Kamieth said. The decision reflects a broader shift in how some German companies think about China as its largest trading partner. Rather than manufacturing primarily in Germany and shipping products eastward, they are increasingly putting production, research and development closer to Chinese customers. Shi Shiwei, director of the Research Center for Europe at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said: "German companies are increasingly embracing a local-for-local strategy, not only selling in China but also conducting research and development, manufacturing, and innovation there. Staying competitive in China can, in turn, strengthen their competitiveness globally." Trempel said China remains an "indispensable market" for key German industries including machinery, automobiles, chemicals and electrical engineering. Its scale can help German companies lower costs and maintain global competitiveness, while Chinese ecosystems in electric mobility, batteries, renewable energy and digital infrastructure also offer opportunities for technological cooperation. The same logic extends beyond traditional heavy industry. For Bayer, another German industrial heavyweight, China is increasingly important, not simply because of the size of its pharmaceutical market, but because of what is being invented there. The company has been expanding an innovation network that links Chinese biotech companies, universities, and research institutions with Bayer's global pharmaceutical development system. In late May, Bayer held an R&D Open Day at the Beijing center, describing China as an integral part of its pharmaceutical research strategy. Stefan Oelrich, a member of the board of management of Bayer AG and head of its Pharmaceuticals Division, told China Daily that China has "one of the most dynamic innovation systems in the pharmaceuticals industry". "China's pharmaceuticals market is, and will remain, a strategic priority for Bayer, and we are continuing to deepen our innovation footprint there," Oelrich said. The shift in language is significant. Bayer no longer describes China only as a destination for medicines developed elsewhere. "Innovation capabilities in China are a strategic pillar of Bayer's global innovation strategy," Oelrich said. "We see China not only as one of our most important markets, but increasingly as an innovation engine feeding directly into our global pipeline." China's biotech industry, academic institutions, clinical capabilities, and digital infrastructure would therefore remain central to Bayer's long-term strategy, he said. "If we want to remain at the forefront of our industry, we need to be where innovation happens. China is clearly one of those places, and an increasingly important one." A similar message has come from Bosch. The German engineering and technology group established the Bosch Robotics Center China in January, focusing on embodied artificial intelligence and humanoid robotics. The company hopes to combine its own expertise in sensors, software, drives and industrial automation with China's manufacturing capacity, supply chains, industrial data and rapidly developing robotics ecosystem. "China is a source of highly qualified talent and strong innovative capacity," then Bosch chairman Stefan Hartung told China Daily at the company's annual media day in April this year. "The Chinese market has requirements unlike those in almost any other market, and this leads to enormous customer focus, great speed, and intense competition." Adapting to circumstances Despite operating in different industries, BASF, Bayer, and Bosch have each made moves that have culminated in a turn toward China. For some of Germany's biggest industrial companies, the country is evolving from primarily a sales market into a place where products are manufactured, technologies developed and new business models tested. The attraction is easy to understand. China, the world's second-largest economy, expanded by 5 percent in 2025. With its vast consumer market, complete manufacturing ecosystem and rapidly developing innovation landscape, the country remains difficult for German industry to ignore despite growing competition and geopolitical uncertainties. Behind the trust is the unusually broad and dense industrial ecosystem of China, which brings together suppliers of sensors, electronics, batteries, motors, precision components and production equipment with software developers and engineering talent, thus creating convenience and lowering costs. In a report published last year, Reuters cited a source as saying that iPhone manufacturing costs in India remained 5 to 8 percent higher than in China, with the gap reaching as much as 10 percent in some cases. Semiconductor industry analyst Chen Jing said the experience-curve concept developed by Bruce Henderson at Boston Consulting Group in the 1960s holds that production costs fall by 10 to 15 percent each time cumulative industrial output doubles. " That rule applies accurately today to China, because other economies cannot match its ability to spread costs across such enormous production volumes, making it highly attractive to investors from major European economies." Pragmatic new ties But the economic relationship is not becoming simpler. German exports to China fell by more than 12 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to less than 37 billion euros, even as German exports overall rose 3.7 percent. Chinese companies, meanwhile, have become challengers in sectors once regarded as German industrial strongholds. Thomas Konig, senior China affairs expert at the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry, or DIHK, sees less contradiction in those trends than the headline numbers might suggest. "Despite geopolitical headwinds, China remains a vital market," Konig told China Daily. "Over 50 percent of German companies operating here state that the Chinese market is of central importance to their global competitiveness." The era in which foreign companies could count on rapid, double-digit Chinese growth may have passed, he said, but that does not make China less relevant. Instead, it is changing the nature of the relationship. "The overall outlook is one of cautious optimism. The era of breakneck, double-digit growth may be over, but a new chapter is beginning," Konig said. German companies' role in China is changing, Konig pointed out, saying: "German companies are no longer just selling to China; they are innovating in and with China to strengthen their competitiveness here and globally." For decades, one of the simplest descriptions of Sino-German economic relations was that Germany sold machinery, automobiles, chemicals and other sophisticated industrial products to a rapidly industrializing China, said Jian Junbo, a professor and the director of Center for China-Europe Relations, Fudan University. Shi Shiwei echoed this. "The China-Germany economic relationship was traditionally seen as highly complementary, with China providing a vast market and manufacturing capacity while Germany supplied sophisticated products in sectors such as automobiles, machinery and chemicals," Shi said. "But as Chinese companies become increasingly competitive in electric vehicles, machinery, green technologies and other fields, the relationship is evolving into one characterized by complementarity, competition and cooperation at the same time." The fact that China is not only a consumer but also a producer, technology developer, and increasingly powerful challenger is described by Trempel as a "paradigm shift" for German business: from "Made in Germany for China" toward "local for local". German companies are increasingly conducting research and development in China rather than merely adapting products developed in Germany. Shorter development cycles — particularly in electric vehicles, batteries, software, and AI — are encouraging them to use Chinese supplier ecosystems and digital platforms, he said. At the same time, the flow of knowledge is becoming more two-way. Innovations developed under China's intense competition and cost pressure can increasingly feed back into products for European and global markets. Konig pointed to smart manufacturing, medical technology, renewable energy and the circular economy as areas offering considerable scope for deeper cooperation. "From electric mobility to industrial efficiency, from medical care to smart AI programs, there remains substantial room for German and Chinese companies to work together," he said. That assessment closely resembles what German executives themselves are doing, but none of the experts interviewed suggested ignoring the difficulties facing China-Germany economic relations. Konig said German companies continue to seek greater market access and better treatment, more transparent regulatory processes and reliable intellectual-property protection. Export controls on rare earths are another immediate concern. "German companies need to continue adapting to the demands of the Chinese market to remain competitive," he said. "The governments of both sides must help to set guardrails for this cooperation and to protect the interests of their respective companies." Trempel likewise argued that closer cooperation comes with risks ranging from unequal market access to geopolitical tensions and competitive pressure. But he rejected the idea that risk reduction should become an argument for dismantling economic ties. Risk assessment, he said, has always been part of business. Companies routinely decide where risks are acceptable and where they are not. For Germany, he argued, the more sustainable approach is to protect genuinely critical technologies and infrastructure while continuing cooperation in areas where the two sides have common interests. "A pragmatic deepening of cooperation can serve as a catalyst for recovery, provided it is accompanied by fair framework conditions," Trempel said. For Konig, the same pragmatism is visible in companies' long-term commitment to China. "From a German business perspective, our commitment to this market is pragmatic, strategic, and long-term," he said. zhangzhouxiang@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Tunneling the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
Built meter by meter: Tunneling the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway Share - WeChat
"A 12.4-kilometer tunnel is built meter by meter." At the Naryn No 1 Tunnel, a key section of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway, China Daily reporter Peng Yixuan speaks with Chinese frontline builders in Kyrgyzstan about life on location and the railway construction process. Against harsh mountain conditions, these workers spare no effort in constructing this critical cross-border rail link. Connecting three nations, the railway boosts regional connectivity and serves as a great example of Belt and Road win-win cooperation.

item.title: Qingdao 'city drink': Brewing coastal charm
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-28
In Qingdao, East China's Shandong province, the sea breeze carries the aroma of malt through century-old breweries, historic streets and crowds gathering at summer dusk. "Drink beer and eat clams", as the local saying goes, has long been part of everyday life in this coastal city. Start the day with a fresh brew and a refreshing spirit. Step into the Tsingtao Beer Museum to witness traditional beer-making techniques meet modern technology, and savor diverse flavors born from different brewing methods. Wander through the liyuan courtyards in Dabao Island, where Chinese and Western architectural styles blend with the city's everyday bustle. Join host Melissa on a 24-hour "city drink" journey through Qingdao and discover the romance of late summer!

item.title: Information resilience need of the hour
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-28
Former Kyrgyz ambassador: Information resilience need of the hour Share - WeChat
Artificial intelligence is making disinformation appear increasingly convincing. Text, images and videos can now be harder than ever to distinguish from the real thing. What does this mean for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, which brings together 10 member states representing more than 3 billion people? Kairat Osmonaliev, former ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary of the Kyrgyz Republic to the Republic of Azerbaijan and concurrently to Georgia, shared his answer in an interview with China Daily's Global Lens: the key is not to establish a common mechanism for controlling information, but to build a system of information resilience among member states, thereby safeguarding the information security of the internet.
